hints: Look closely at the labels on the right-hand cell. Y is inside the cytoplasm and Z is outside in the cell wall space, so ask yourself which cell must be the companion cell doing the pumping.
Remember how sucrose is loaded at the source. Protons are first pumped out using ATP, then allowed back in together with sucrose, so which movement needs active transport?
walkthrough:
**Identify the two cells and the spaces**

The cell on the right with Y inside and Z outside is the companion cell. Y is its cytoplasm and Z is the apoplast outside its cell membrane. The cell on the left is the sieve tube element, and W and X are linked by plasmodesmata.

**Recall proton pumping for loading**

To load sucrose, the companion cell uses ATP to pump hydrogen ions, protons ($H^+$), out of its cytoplasm into the surrounding cell wall space. This builds up a high concentration of protons outside. That is:
$$cytoplasm (Y) \rightarrow apoplast (Z) \text{ by active transport}$$

**Link the gradient to sucrose movement**

The proton gradient is then used to bring sucrose back into the companion cell by proton-sucrose co-transport, and sucrose then diffuses through plasmodesmata from the companion cell (X side) into the sieve tube element (W side). So the only active step described correctly is protons Y to Z.

options.A: Sucrose is not pumped from Y to Z. Sucrose moves from the apoplast into the companion cell, the opposite direction, and by co-transport not by direct active transport.
options.B: This is the proton pump. ATP in the companion cell actively pumps protons from cytoplasm Y out to the apoplast Z to create the gradient for loading.
options.C: Protons do move back from Z to Y, but not by simple diffusion. They return through a specific co-transporter protein together with sucrose.
options.D: Movement from X to W through plasmodesmata is sucrose moving by diffusion down its concentration gradient, not protons moving by diffusion.
